name: Ancient India
summary: Beginning with Chandragupta Maurya's conquest of Magadha and Ashoka's embrace of Buddhism after the brutal Kalinga War, ancient India's classical age unfolds through nearly five centuries of shifting successor kingdoms -- Shunga, Satavahana, Indo-Greek, and Kushan -- before the Gupta dynasty ushers in a golden age of Sanskrit literature, mathematics, and monumental architecture, ending amid Hunnic invasions and fragmentation around 550 CE.
imageAttribution: Photo by Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The North Gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, a Buddhist monument begun under the Maurya Empire.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
events.body: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nanda Empire and seizes Magadha, founding the Maurya Empire, which grows into the first empire to unify most of the Indian subcontinent.
events.imageAttribution: Stamp design by Garudam, GODL-India, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 2001 Indian postage stamp depicting Chandragupta Maurya, founder of the Maurya Empire.

events.title: The Kalinga War
events.body: Ashoka's Maurya army conquers the independent kingdom of Kalinga in a brutal war; the scale of the bloodshed later drives Ashoka toward Buddhism and nonviolence.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bhajish Bharathan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ashoka's rock edicts at Dhauli, inscribed near the site of the Kalinga War.

events.title: Ashoka converts to Buddhism and issues his edicts
events.body: Remorseful after Kalinga, Ashoka embraces Buddhism and begins inscribing edicts of dharma on rocks and pillars across the empire, promoting nonviolence, religious tolerance, and public welfare.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sachin kumar tiwary, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: One of Ashoka's pillar edicts, at Lauriya Areraj in Bihar.

events.title: Ashoka commissions the Great Stupa at Sanchi
events.body: Ashoka has a hemispherical brick stupa built at Sanchi to house relics of the Buddha, the first monument on a hilltop site that grows into one of Buddhism's great architectural complexes.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Ashokan-era pillar standing at the Great Stupa site in Sanchi.

events.title: Pushyamitra Shunga overthrows the Maurya Empire
events.body: Pushyamitra Shunga, a Mauryan military commander, assassinates the last Mauryan emperor Brihadratha during a troop review and founds the Shunga Empire in Magadha, ending a century of Mauryan rule.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Dhanadeva-Ayodhya inscription, a 1st-century BCE epigraph naming the Shunga dynasty.

events.title: Menander I converts to Buddhism
events.body: The Indo-Greek king Menander I, ruling from Sagala in the Punjab, embraces Buddhism after a recorded dialogue with the monk Nagasena, becoming a celebrated patron of the faith in the Hellenistic-influenced northwest.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by CNG Coins, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin portrait of the Indo-Greek king Menander I.

events.title: The Satavahana dynasty is founded
events.body: Simuka establishes the Satavahana dynasty in the Deccan, filling the power vacuum left by Maurya collapse and building a long-lived kingdom that dominates central and southern India for over three centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Uploadalt, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of the later Satavahana king Vashishtiputra Sri Satakarni, photographed at the British Museum.

events.title: Ornamental gateways rise at the Sanchi Stupa
events.body: Under Satavahana patronage, elaborately carved stone gateways depicting scenes from the Buddha's life are added to the Great Stupa at Sanchi, replacing its simpler earlier entrances.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The carved Eastern Gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi.

events.title: Kujula Kadphises unifies the Kushan Empire
events.body: Kujula Kadphises unites the five Yuezhi tribes of Bactria under his rule, founding the Kushan Empire, which soon expands south across the Hindu Kush into the Indian subcontinent.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by Classical Numismatic Group, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A tetradrachm coin of the Kushan king Kujula Kadphises.

events.title: Kanishka becomes Kushan emperor
events.body: Kanishka takes the Kushan throne and rules from twin capitals at Purushapura and Mathura, presiding over the empire's territorial and commercial peak along the Silk Road.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gold coin of Kanishka, held at the British Museum.

events.title: Kanishka convenes a great Buddhist council in Kashmir
events.body: Kanishka sponsors a gathering of Buddhist scholars in Kashmir, remembered in tradition as the Fourth Buddhist Council, that produces authoritative commentaries on Buddhist scripture and helps carry Buddhism along Central Asian trade routes.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain (Peshawar Museum, 1930), via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Buddhist sculptural group from the Peshawar Museum, from the Gandhara region patronized under Kanishka.

events.title: The Gandhara school of Greco-Buddhist art flourishes
events.body: Sculptors in Gandhara, working under Kushan patronage, blend Hellenistic artistic technique inherited from the region's Greek-ruled past with Buddhist subject matter, producing some of the first anthropomorphic images of the Buddha.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by World Imaging, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1st-century Gandharan sculpture of the Buddha in Greco-Buddhist style.

events.title: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire
events.body: Chandragupta I is crowned Maharajadhiraja, marking the start of the Gupta Empire and the Gupta calendar era; his marriage to the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi strengthens the new dynasty's standing in Magadha.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Uploadalt, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gold coin depicting Chandragupta I and Queen Kumaradevi.

events.title: Samudragupta expands the Gupta Empire
events.body: Samudragupta campaigns across northern and southern India, uprooting rival kings and extending Gupta authority from the Himalayas toward the Deccan; his conquests are recorded on the Allahabad Pillar inscription.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of the Gupta emperor Samudragupta.

events.title: Chandragupta II defeats the Western Kshatrapas
events.body: Chandragupta II conquers the Saka Western Kshatrapas of Gujarat and Malwa, giving the Gupta Empire access to the western coast's sea trade and bringing it to its greatest territorial extent.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of Chandragupta II depicted on horseback.

events.title: Sanskrit literature flourishes under Chandragupta II
events.body: The poet-playwright Kalidasa, widely regarded as ancient India's greatest Sanskrit writer, is thought to have composed his major works during Chandragupta II's reign, part of a broader flowering of Sanskrit literature and drama under Gupta patronage.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by William Douglas Almond, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An early-20th-century illustration imagining Kalidasa composing verse.

events.title: The Iron Pillar is forged under Chandragupta II
events.body: Metalworkers cast a 7-metre iron pillar honoring Chandragupta II, using a corrosion-resistant alloy that keeps the column virtually rust-free some sixteen centuries later -- a landmark of Gupta-era metallurgy.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mark A. Wilson, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Iron Pillar, now standing in the Qutb complex in Delhi.

events.title: Kumaragupta I founds Nalanda
events.body: Kumaragupta I endows a monastery at Nalanda that grows into the ancient world's foremost center of learning, drawing students and scholars from across Asia to study Buddhist philosophy alongside grammar, medicine, and logic.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Odantapuribs, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of Temple No. 3 at the Nalanda archaeological site.

events.title: Skandagupta repels a Hunnic invasion
events.body: Skandagupta defeats an invasion by Hunnic raiders, probably the Kidarites, restoring Gupta military prestige at the start of his reign even as the empire's northwestern frontier comes under growing pressure.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by CNG Coins, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A coin of Skandagupta, shown holding a bow and arrow.

events.title: Aryabhata completes the Aryabhatiya
events.body: Working at Kusumapura, Aryabhata completes the Aryabhatiya, a landmark treatise that lays out a decimal place-value number system, calculates pi to four decimal places, and explains solar and lunar eclipses through the Earth's rotation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Cpjha13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern statue of Aryabhata in Bihar.

events.title: Mihirakula's Huna forces overrun Gupta's northwest
events.body: The Alchon Hun king Mihirakula conquers Sindh and pushes into Punjab and Kashmir, breaking Gupta control over the subcontinent's northwest and accelerating the empire's fragmentation.
events.imageAttribution: Coin photo by CNG Coins, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A numismatic portrait of the Alchon Hun king Mihirakula.

events.title: The Gupta Empire fragments and falls
events.body: Weakened by decades of Hunnic incursions and the rise of regional rivals such as Yashodharman, the Gupta Empire fades into a scatter of successor kingdoms; Vishnugupta, the last recognized ruler of the main line, issues his final inscription around this time.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Koba-chan, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the Gupta Empire's extent around 420 CE, before its later fragmentation.
